content.text: Resource Mobilization, Monetary Architecture, Fiscal Mechanics, and Capital Markets in India

Resource mobilization encompasses the mechanisms by which a developing economy channels domestic savings, tax revenues, non-debt capital, and external financial inflows into productive capital formation. In India, this involves an intricate coordination between the fiscal policy of the Ministry of Finance and the monetary policy of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), structured alongside public debt management and financial market deepening.

content.text: 1. Sources of Financial Resources: Public vs. Private Mobilization

content.caption: Key Channels of Resource Mobilization in the Indian Economy
rows: Public Sector: Tax Revenues
Direct Taxes (Corporation Tax, Personal Income Tax); Indirect Taxes (GST, Customs, Central Excise on petroleum/liquor).
Gross Tax-to-GDP ratio stands around 11.5%–12.0%. Personal income tax collections have outpaced corporate tax collections due to formalization and digital TDS/TCS tracking.
Narrow direct tax base (~2.5% of population effectively pay income tax); high agricultural exemption; litigation delays under Vivad se Vishwas.
Public Sector: Non-Tax & Capital Receipts
Dividends from PSUs & RBI surplus transfers; spectrum auctions; disinvestment/privatization receipts; National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP).
RBI dividend transfers (record ₹2.11 lakh crore in FY24) provide crucial fiscal cushion. Asset monetization favored over outright strategic disinvestment.
Disinvestment targets frequently missed; market valuation cyclicality; public resistance to privatization of strategic CPSEs.
Public Debt & Deficit Financing
Internal Debt: Dated Government Securities (G-Secs), Treasury Bills (91, 182, 364 days), Small Savings Schemes (NSC, PPF). External Debt: Multilateral/bilateral loans (World Bank, ADB, JICA).
General Government Debt-to-GDP ratio elevated around 81%–83% post-pandemic. Target under NK Singh Committee FRBM recommendation is 60% (40% Centre, 20% States).
Deficit financing via direct monetization (RBI printing currency) discontinued since 1997 WMA agreement; fiscal deficit financed entirely through market borrowings, pushing yield curve pressures.
External Foreign Flows: FDI vs. FPI
FDI: Long-term equity in manufacturing, services, infrastructure via Automatic & Government approval routes. FPI/FII: Portfolio flows in equities and G-Secs via SEBI registration.

Gross FDI inflows average $70–$80 billion annually, with Singapore, Mauritius, and USA as top source jurisdictions. Indian Sovereign G-Sec inclusion in global bond indices (J.P. Morgan GBI-EM, Bloomberg).
FPI represents 'hot money' vulnerable to US Fed interest rate cycles and global geopolitical volatility, inducing Rupee exchange rate shocks.

content.text: 2. Monetary Policy Architecture & RBI Policy Transmission
Under the amended Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (Finance Act 2016), India instituted a statutory Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) transitioning to a Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) regime:

items: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): Comprises 6 members—3 internal (RBI Governor as ex-officio Chairperson with casting vote, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, and one RBI official) and 3 external members nominated by the Central Government for a 4-year non-renewable term.

Inflation Mandate: Statutory target of 4% Headline CPI inflation with a tolerance corridor of +/- 2% (2% to 6%). Breaching the target for 3 consecutive quarters triggers mandatory written reporting to Parliament specifying causes and remedial timelines.

Monetary Policy Instruments: Quantitative tools include Policy Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, Standing Deposit Facility (SDF, uncollateralized liquidity absorption rate introduced in 2022), Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR, currently 18%).

External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR): Mandatory since October 2019 for floating rate retail and MSME loans, linking bank lending rates directly to external benchmarks (Repo rate or T-Bill yields) to eliminate the sluggish transmission observed under the Base Rate and MCLR regimes.

content.text: 3. Financial Sector Ecosystem: Commercial Banks, NBFCs & DFIs

content.caption: Pillars of the Indian Financial Intermediation System
headers: Role in Capital Formation & Systemic Fragilities
rows: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs)
Regulated under Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI Act, 1934. Subject to Basel III Capital Adequacy (CRAR min 9% + CCB).

Primary credit dispensers; transformed post-consolidation (mega-mergers of PSBs in 2020) and IBC clean-up; priority sector lending (PSL) target of 40% for domestic banks drives credit to agriculture and weaker sections.
Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)
Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework by RBI (Base, Middle, Upper, and Top Layers).

Specialized last-mile credit delivery in auto loans, microfinance, and real estate; liquidity shocks (IL&FS crisis 2018, DHFL) prompted tighter asset-liability management (ALM) guidelines and Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework extension to NBFCs.
Development Financial Institutions (DFIs)
National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) established under NaBFID Act, 2021.

Revival of long-term development financing to tackle the severe maturity mismatch in commercial bank infrastructure lending; mandated to catalyze ₹5 lakh crore+ debt financing for the National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP).

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Explain the statutory framework of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in India. How has the shift to the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) improved monetary policy transmission? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Trace the evolution from the Urjit Patel Committee recommendations to the 2016 RBI Act amendment; outline the 6-member MPC composition, voting rules, and the 4% (+/- 2%) CPI mandate; analyze the shortcomings of historical lending mechanisms (PLR, Base Rate, MCLR) which permitted asymmetrical transmission; elucidate EBLR mechanics linking retail/MSME advances to Repo or T-Bill yields; evaluate outcomes: faster rate pass-through during monetary tightening and easing cycles, alongside challenges like increased interest rate volatility for retail borrowers.

Critically evaluate the significance of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in last-mile credit delivery and the regulatory rationale behind RBI's Scale-Based Regulatory (SBR) framework. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Highlight NBFC strengths in niche credit assessment, unbanked segments, microfinance, and MSME clusters; discuss systemic contagion risks revealed by the 2018 IL&FS and DHFL collapses (asset-liability mismatch, short-term commercial papers financing long-term real estate); explain RBI's four-tiered Scale-Based Regulation (Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer, Top Layer) based on asset size, activity, and systemic risk; conclude on balancing financial stability with entrepreneurial credit expansion.

Discuss the rationale for establishing the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID). Why did commercial banks struggle with infrastructure financing in India? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Define the asset-liability mismatch (ALM) confronting commercial banks whose liabilities are short-term deposits (1-3 years) while infrastructure assets require long-term gestation (15-25 years); examine how this structural flaw precipitated the 2012-2018 NPA crisis; explain the mandate, capital structure, and regulatory exemptions of NaBFID under the 2021 Act; assess NaBFID's catalytic role in mobilizing patient capital, pension/insurance funds, and bond market integration.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which instrument was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in April 2022 to absorb liquidity from commercial banks without requiring collateral G-Secs?
(a) Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)
(b) Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)
(c) Liquidity Adjustment Facility Repo
(d) Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR)
Correct Answer: (b) Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) [Explanation: The SDF was operationalized at 25 bps below the policy repo rate as an uncollateralized liquidity absorption mechanism under amended Section 17 of the RBI Act.]

Q2. What is the statutory target for Priority Sector Lending (PSL) prescribed by the RBI for domestic scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs and Small Finance Banks)?
(a) 25% of ANBC
(b) 30% of ANBC
(c) 40% of ANBC
(d) 50% of ANBC
Correct Answer: (c) 40% of ANBC [Explanation: Domestic commercial banks must allocate 40% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE) to designated priority sectors.]

Q3. Who among the following possesses a second or 'casting vote' in the statutory Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in case of a tie?
(a) Union Finance Minister
(b) Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs
(c) Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
(d) Senior-most external member of MPC
Correct Answer: (c) Governor of the Reserve Bank of India [Explanation: Under Section 45ZL of the RBI Act, each member of the MPC has one vote, and in case of an equality of votes, the Governor has a second or casting vote.]

Q4. Under the recommendations of the N.K. Singh Committee on FRBM, what was the recommended debt-to-GDP ceiling for the General Government by FY 2023?
(a) 40% of GDP
(b) 50% of GDP
(c) 60% of GDP (40% Centre and 20% States)
(d) 70% of GDP
Correct Answer: (c) 60% of GDP (40% Centre and 20% States) [Explanation: The FRBM Review Committee led by N.K. Singh recommended a debt-to-GDP target of 60% for the combined government by 2023, comprising 40% for the Union and 20% for the States.]

Q5. Which financial institution was established by Parliament in 2021 as the apex Development Financial Institution (DFI) for infrastructure financing?
(a) IDFC First Bank
(b) NaBFID (National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development)
(c) IIFCL
(d) IRFC
Correct Answer: (b) NaBFID [Explanation: NaBFID was established under the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development Act, 2021 as a specialized DFI to support the National Infrastructure Pipeline.]
